newsitem.title: USA: Narrow WTI/Brent cuts N.Sea crude offerings to US.
newsitem.headline: Narrow WTI/Brent cuts N.Sea crude offerings to US.

text.p: A narrowing of the transatlantic arbitrage cut off some of the North Sea crude offerings on the Gulf Coast on Monday, but U.S. refiners still had plenty of barrels from which to choose, traders said.
The spread between West Texas Intermediate/Cushing and Brent was around $1.40-50 on Monday afternoon, down some 20-30 cents from recent days, traders said.
The changing economics of bringing Brent to the U.S. was exasperated by Shell Oil Co's failure of VLCC Berge Nisa that had been destined for the U.S. market, traders said.

Koch Oil was considered the only major player in town in terms of Brent. The benchmark was heard offered at 60 cents under WTI/Cushing for first-half July delivery, up five to 10 cents from last week.
The narrowing arbitrage was expected to show up in stronger diferentials for domestic alternative Light Louisiana Sweet/St. James and regional sweets like Colombian Cusiana.

West African barrels, however, remained abundant. Nigerian grades Brass River and Bonny Light were assessed around WTI plus 10 cents a barrel for third-decade June and second-decade July delivery, respectively, traders said.
Various Qua Iboe cargoes were also looking for homes in July around parity with WTI.
A Saharan Blend cargo for early June arrival was distressed in light of the lack of storage on the Gulf Coast. The last formal offer heard was around $1.25 under WTI/Cushing.

Many refiners were looking for spare storage. Most tankage is already full, much of it attributed to foreign barrels likely to be delivered against the July NYMEX crude contract that expires on June 20.

Finally, sources said the U.S. is likely to support renewal of the Iraqi oil-for-food deal, following up on U.N. Secretary General Kofi Annan's recommendation that the deal be renewed for six months under the current $2 billion ceiling.
The current deal expires on June 7.
